newsitem.title: FRANCE: Beaten French Gaullist party chief Mancel quits.
newsitem.headline: Beaten French Gaullist party chief Mancel quits.

text.p: The secretary-general of the French Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party, Jean-Francois Mancel, resigned on Monday following his party's crushing defeat at the polls by a Socialist-led left-wing coalition.

Mancel, who lost his own parliamentary seat in Sunday's general election rout, handed in his resignation in a letter to outgoing prime minister Alain Juppe, the RPR president, the text of which was released to the press.
"It seems normal that our movement, which will now write a new page in its history, should do so under the leadership of a new team," Mancel wrote to Juppe.
The resignation clearly portended a re-structuring of the shell-shocked French Right, including the RPR, in the wake of Sunday's stunning left-wing election victory.

Earlier on Monday President Jacques Chirac, the RPR's founder, was obliged to name victorious Socialist leader Lionel Jospin as his next prime minister. Jospin will now "cohabit" with the humiliated Chirac, whose term has five years to run.
Several RPR notables called on Juppe during the day, among them outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin who had been tipped to succeed him had the Right won the election.

Seguin, long a rival of Juppe's, made no comment after their meeting but L'Est Republicain, the main newspaper serving Seguin's east France power base, said he had predicted virtual bloodshed in the fight for control of the party.
The daily said Seguin had spoken of a "knife fight to the finish" to wrest leadership of the RPR away from Juppe.
It quoted Seguin as saying: "Juppe and the others like him want to keep control of the RPR as if nothing had happened but I'm going to kick in the ant hill."
Seguin, in words already widely seen as a challenge to Juppe, said on Sunday night he was "definitely determined to create the political conditions to prepare other, better days for France."
Juppe, clearly seeking to protect his position, met earlier with former minister Nicolas Sarkozy, until now a close aide to former RPR premier Edouard Balladur, another leadership rival.
The jockeying for power within the RPR was mirrored in the higher reaches of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF), the RPR's partner in the former ruling coalition.
Three faction leaders, Francois Leotard, Francois Bayrou and Alain Madelin, all made statements indicating that the loose-knit grouping was also on the verge of breaking up.
